textbookText: G0 - Phase: In the G0 phase, cells are inactive due to the unavailability of mitogens and energy-rich compounds. Despite their metabolic activity, they function as reserve cells poised to re-enter the cell cycle. The transition from G1 to G2 is linked to cell differentiation. Cell cycle durations vary based on cell type and external factors, with the G phase occupying 30-40%, the S phase 30-50%, the C phase 1020%, and the M phase 5-10% of the total duration.

INDIRECT CELL DIVISION Mitosis, also known as indirect cell division, ensures that daughter cells, resulting from the division of a mature cell, possess the same chromosome number as the mother cell. This process occurs in somatic cells during growth, germ cells in the gonads, meristematic cells in plants, and during embryonic development. The steps of mitotic cell division involve duplicating all cell contents, including chromosomes, and carefully controlled splitting to form two identical daughter cells. 1. Karyokinesis 2. Cytokinesis A. Interphase: It is the stage between two successive cell multiplications. During the

stage, the cell is metabolically very active despite appearing restful. Key features of this stage include: The following observations are characteristic of this stage: i. Chromosomes can be observed in diffused, long and coiled chromatin fibers. ii. Chromosomes form their exact copies. iii. Synthesis of protein and RNA occurs. iv. Duplication of cell organelles such as mitochondria, plastids, and centrioles takes place.
Fig. 1.3.3 Interphase B. Mitotic phase 1. Karyokinesis: (Greek, karyon = nucleus; kinesis = movement) The division of nucleus comprises four phases:

a. Prophase (G., 'pro' = first, 'phasis' = stage): The initial visible step in nuclear division involves several changes which are characterized by following key events: i. The nucleus becomes spheroid and viscosity of cytoplasm increases. ii. DNA molecules condense to form elongated chromosomes which further shorten and thicken by the assistance of protein condensins. iii. Each chromosome contains two sister chromatids connected at a point called centromere. iv. In animal cells, two centrosomes (each with a pair of centrioles) start moving to opposite poles. Both centriole pairs radiate fine microtubular fibrils which is known as astral rays.

v. By the end of this phase, nucleoli and nuclear membrane disintergrate and completely disspear; asters (centriole pairs with astral rays) lie at the region of future spindle poles.

Fig. 1.3.3 Prophase b. Metaphase (G., 'meta' = after, 'phasis' = stage): Metaphase marks the initial visible step in nuclear division, characterized by the following key events: i. All chromosomes lie at equatorial region in a single alignment called metaphasic plate. ii. Each chromosome, at centromere, is attached to both spindle poles by Spindle fibers. This process of bringing the chromosomes to equator is called congression. iii. Smaller chromosomes lie towards the centre while larger ones lie at periphery.

Fig. 1.3.3 Metaphase c. Anaphase (G., ana = up; phasis = stage): Anaphase, also known as migratory phase, is the shortest phase characterized by the following key events: i. The Centromere of each chromosome splits, forming two sister chromatids which later become daughter chromosomes. ii. These daughter chromosomes, each with a single chromatid, move towards opposite poles due to the contraction of spindle fibers and the stretch developed in the interzonal region.
